message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on the specific analytical context—what you’re measuring, how you’ll prepare the sample, what instrumentation you have, and what performance metrics (sensitivity, selectivity, speed, robustness) matter most.** Below is a quick‑reference guide that outlines the most common ionisation techniques, their strengths/weaknesses, and typical use‑cases. Use it as a decision tree: start with your analyte class and sample matrix, then narrow down to the method that best matches your needs. | Ionisation Technique | Principle | Typical Mass‑Spec Platforms | Strengths | Weaknesses | Best‑For | |----------------------|-----------|-----------------------------|-----------|------------|----------| | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Charged droplets → desolvation → ions | LC‑MS/MS, LC‑MS, LC‑MSⁿ | • Soft, preserves non‑covalent complexes
• Good for polar, high‑molecular‑weight molecules (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids)
• Compatible with liquid chromatography | • Requires aqueous/organic solvent mixtures
• Susceptible to ion suppression from salts, detergents
• Limited for very non‑polar compounds | • Proteomics, metabolomics, pharmaceuticals, biomarker discovery | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Laser + matrix → desorption/ionisation | MALDI‑TOF, MALDI‑TOF/TOF, MALDI‑MS/MS | • Very soft, minimal fragmentation
• Handles large biomolecules (proteins, polymers)
• Fast, high‑throughput (spot‑by‑spot) | • Requires matrix selection; matrix ions can interfere at low m/z
• Less quantitative than ESI
• Sample prep can be laborious | • Protein fingerprinting, peptide sequencing, polymer analysis, imaging MS | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Corona discharge → gas‑phase ionisation | LC‑MS/MS, LC‑MS | • Soft, good for moderately polar to non‑polar small molecules
• Works with high organic content solvents
• Less ion suppression than ESI | • Not ideal for very polar or high‑MW analytes
• Requires a nebuliser and gas flow | • Lipids, steroids, small drug molecules, environmental contaminants | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | UV photons → photoionisation | LC‑MS/MS, LC‑MS | • Excellent for non‑polar, aromatic compounds
• Complementary to APCI/ESI | • Requires dopants for some analytes
• Less common, limited instrument availability | • Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides, pharmaceuticals | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Reagent gas (e.g., methane, ammonia) → proton transfer | GC‑MS, GC‑MS/MS | • Soft, reduces fragmentation
• Good for GC‑compatible analytes | • Requires GC, not suitable for thermally labile or high‑MW species | • Volatile organics, environmental samples | | **Electron Ionisation (EI)** | High‑energy electrons → ionisation | GC‑MS, GC‑MS/MS | • Standardised, reproducible fragmentation patterns
• Good library matching | • Hard ionisation → extensive fragmentation (hard to detect intact ions)
• Requires volatile, thermally stable analytes | • Small volatile molecules, forensic, environmental | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photo‑Ionisation (APPI)** | UV photons + dopant → ionisation | LC‑MS | • Good for non‑polar, aromatic compounds | • Requires dopants, less common | • Pesticides, PAHs | | **Desorption Electrospray Ionisation (DESI)** | Ambient ionisation via charged spray | Ambient MS, imaging | • No sample prep, real‑time analysis | • Lower sensitivity, limited to surface analysis | • Forensic, cultural heritage, rapid screening | | **Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS)** | Ion beam sputtering → secondary ions | Surface analysis | • Extremely high spatial resolution | • Limited to surface layers, destructive | • Materials science, semiconductor, surface chemistry | --- ## Decision Flow 1. **What is the analyte?** - **Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides, glycans, DNA)** → **ESI** (LC‑MS/MS) or **MALDI** (TOF). - **Small polar molecules (metabolites, drugs)** → **ESI** (LC‑MS/MS). - **Non‑polar, aromatic small molecules (PAHs, pesticides)** → **APCI** or **APPI** (LC‑MS). - **Volatile, thermally stable organics** → **EI** (GC‑MS). - **Thermally labile or high‑MW organics** → **CI** (GC‑MS) or **APCI** (LC‑MS). 2. **Sample matrix** - **Complex biological fluids (serum, plasma)** → **ESI** (LC‑MS/MS) with solid‑phase extraction or protein precipitation. - **Solid or semi‑solid samples (tissue, polymers)** → **MALDI** (TOF) or **SIMS**. - **Ambient or on‑site analysis** → **DESI** or **DART** (not listed above but similar). 3. **Quantitative vs. qualitative** - **Quantitative, high precision** → **ESI** (LC‑MS/MS) with isotope‑labeled standards. - **Rapid screening, fingerprinting** → **MALDI** (TOF) or **DESI**. 4. **Instrument availability** - If you only have a GC‑MS, use **EI** or **CI**. - If you have an LC‑MS/MS, **ESI** is usually the default; add **APCI/APPI** if you need to cover non‑polar analytes. 5. **Sensitivity requirements** - **Ultra‑low limits (pM–fM)** → **ESI** (LC‑MS/MS) with nano‑LC or capillary‑ESI. - **High throughput** → **MALDI** (TOF) or **DESI**. --- ## Quick Recommendations | Scenario | Recommended Ionisation | |----------|------------------------| | **Proteomics (peptide sequencing)** | ESI (LC‑MS/MS) | | **Protein fingerprinting** | MALDI‑TOF | | **Metabolomics (polar metabolites)** | ESI (LC‑MS/MS) | | **Lipids (non‑polar)** | APCI (LC‑MS/MS) | | **Pesticides (aromatic, non‑polar)** | APPI (LC‑MS/MS) | | **Volatile organics (forensics)** | EI (GC‑MS) | | **Thermally labile organics** | CI (GC‑MS) | | **Rapid on‑site screening** | DESI (ambient MS) | | **Surface analysis** | SIMS | --- ### Bottom Line - **ESI** is the workhorse for most liquid‑chromatography‑based analyses of polar to moderately non‑polar molecules, especially when you need quantitative, high‑sensitivity data. - **MALDI** shines for large biomolecules and high‑throughput fingerprinting. - **APCI/APPI** fill the gap for non‑polar, aromatic small molecules that ESI struggles with. - **EI/CI** are the go‑to for GC‑MS when you need robust, library‑matching fragmentation. Pick the method that aligns with your analyte chemistry, sample matrix, and analytical goals. If you’re still unsure, a quick test run with a few representative standards on each platform can reveal which ionisation gives the best signal‑to‑noise and reproducibility for your specific application.
